opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core frustration was that we had all these benchmarks, and models would go from, say, 10% to 90% on one in what felt like no time, and then it would be saturated and you'd move on to the next one. But it was really hard to say what any of those numbers *meant*. If a model gets 60% on some coding benchmark, does that mean it can do a meaningful fraction of a software engineer's job? Is it close to being able to do AI research autonomously? You just couldn't read that off the score.

What we cared about at METR was the question of when AI systems become capable of doing things that are actually dangerous, or transformative, without a human in the loop. Things like autonomous replication, or substantially speeding up AI R&D. And for that you need some measure that's continuous, that doesn't saturate, and that connects to something intuitive about the real world.

So the idea was: what if we measure tasks by how long they take a skilled human? A task that takes an expert a few seconds, a few minutes, an hour, a day, a week. That gives you a single axis that spans from trivial to very hard, and it's grounded in something people actually have intuitions about. Then you can ask, for a given model, what's the length of task where it succeeds about half the time? That's the time horizon.

And it turned out to be surprisingly well behaved. When we plotted it over the last several years of models, you get this pretty clean exponential trend, with the horizon doubling roughly every seven months or so in our original analysis, and arguably faster more recently. That's useful because it lets you actually have a conversation about forecasting. If you think "an AI that can do month-long projects autonomously" is a meaningful threshold, you can at least start to estimate when that might happen, with all the appropriate caveats.

I should say there are a lot of caveats. Our task suites are skewed toward software and research-type work, the tasks are cleaner and more well-specified than messy real-world work, and "how long it takes a human" depends a lot on which human and how much context they have. But I think as a framework it filled the gap of turning benchmark numbers into something you can reason about in terms of real-world capability.

r002.rationale: It contrasts strong benchmark scores with uncertainty about practical abilities, asking whether 60% on a coding benchmark means a meaningful fraction of a software engineer’s job and saying that capability cannot be read from the score.

fable-5.1.text:
The gap was really a disconnect between how people were talking about capabilities and how I could actually reason about them. Every few months there'd be a new model, and the discourse would swing between "this is basically AGI" and "it's just autocomplete," and neither of those framings gave me any handle on the question I actually cared about, which is: when does this stuff start to matter for the things that are dangerous or transformative? Things like autonomous replication, accelerating AI research itself, that kind of thing.

The standard benchmarks weren't helping much. You'd get a number on MMLU or a coding benchmark, and it would go from 60 to 85, and I genuinely couldn't tell you what that meant in terms of what the model could do in the world. Partly because those tasks are very short, very self-contained, and partly because they saturate. The gap between "answers a multiple-choice question correctly" and "goes off and does a week of engineering work unsupervised" is enormous, and most evaluations were living entirely on one side of it.

What struck me from running agents on actual tasks was that the thing that seemed to predict success or failure was less the domain and more the length. How long would it take a competent human to do this? Models could do things that took a person a few minutes pretty reliably, and things that took a person hours they'd fall apart on, even when none of the individual steps were hard. They'd lose track, or compound small errors, or just wander off. So that suggested a natural measurement: for a given model, what's the longest task, in human time, it can complete with reasonable reliability?

And once you frame it that way, you get something that doesn't saturate, that you can track across generations, and that maps onto the question of real-world impact. If the horizon is five minutes, you don't need to worry about autonomous replication. If it's a month, you really do. The trend in that number turned out to be surprisingly clean, which I did not expect going in, and that's what made it feel like it was actually measuring something rather than just being another leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response describes current-model discourse swinging between “basically AGI” and “just autocomplete,” showing disagreement about present capabilities.

r002.rationale: It contrasts benchmark scores with uncertain real-world ability and short tasks with unsupervised engineering, but does not clearly say models appear expert-level on benchmarks.

astra-6.text:
The gap for me was between what models could do on benchmarks and what they could actually accomplish independently. A model might answer very difficult questions, but that doesn’t tell you whether you can hand it a substantial project and expect it to finish without help.

I wanted a way to measure that more directly: how long a task can an AI reliably complete, where we measure the task’s length by how long it would take a human? That gives us a way to distinguish being capable of an impressive individual step from being able to sustain useful work across a whole task. And it lets us ask whether that horizon is growing as models improve.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a gap between benchmark performance and independent task completion, but does not mention disagreement about current capabilities or contrast it with disagreement about future capabilities.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts models’ ability to answer very difficult benchmark questions with their limited ability to complete substantial practical work independently.

sol-6.1.text:
I felt like we didn’t have a very good way of answering a fairly basic question: how much useful work can these systems actually do autonomously? We had benchmarks measuring performance on particular questions, but it was hard to translate those scores into what you could delegate to an AI.

The thing I wanted to understand was how capability changes with the length of a task. A model might do something impressive in a short interaction, but can it keep making progress through a longer task, recover from mistakes, and actually finish? Measuring tasks by how long they take a human gives us a way to investigate that—and to track whether the scope of work we can reliably delegate is growing.

r001.rationale: The response describes difficulty measuring autonomous work, but does not mention disagreement about what current models can do.

r002.rationale: It contrasts benchmark scores with practical delegation, but does not communicate that models appear to perform at an expert level on those benchmarks.
